Mixed, Transitional, Borderline, and Miscellaneous Groups. $$$ The descriptions of the various conditions dealt with in preceding chapters have been formulated in as clear-cut a manner as possible for didactic purposes. The cases for illustration have been carefully selected, with the same purposes in mind. In practice, however, one soon finds that such clear-cut cases are the exception rather than the rule. In many cases various combinations and sequences of events of pathogenesis and manifestation are seen, necessitating individualization in the diagnostic and therapeutic work. There are a good many cases in which there is such a mixture or alternation of manifestations belonging to 2 different groups that they cannot be definitely assigned to either group, except by some arbitrary policy. Four case examples illustrate this admixture of manifestations and the ensuing diagnostic complexity. The first case is of a 30-year-old male with manic-depressive psychosis complicated with a strong paranoid trend. The second case presents a combination of relative mental deficiency, epileptic seizures over a period of 3 years, and some neurologic residuals, occurring on a complex etiologic basis: cerebral birth trauma, whooping cough with cerebral complications, and epidemic encephalitis in a 10-year-old girl. The third case is of a 32-year-old male with neuropathic heredity, birth injury, chaotic sexuality, antisocial tendencies, alcoholism, maternal fixation, postnatal head injury, marital maladjustment, and cyclothymic traits. The fourth case is of a 35-year-old female with so-called psychopathic personality, a truly unique combination of manifestations. For clinical purposes, in most, if not all, cases, a single-term diagnosis is not of great value. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved) 
Epilepsy (grand mal, petit mal, Jacksonian, and hystero-epilepsy). $$$ Epilepsy is the name applied to a group of conditions which present many manifestations but in which there is usually to be found convulsions and some degree of unconsciousness. It is a chronic disorder of the nervous system, occurs in more or less frequent attacks similar in character, and invariably leads to, or is accompanied by, some measure of mental abnormality. Every convulsion does not mean epilepsy and there even are types of epilepsy where the convulsions are absent. Epilepsy has been variously classified and, in fact, it would be better to speak of the "epilepsies" in order to emphasize the different manifestations. The commonest, and also perhaps the most convenient from the clinical psychologist's point of view, is a classification according to manifestations shown-in other words, according to symptoms. Such a symptomatic grouping is as follows: grand mal, petit mal, Jacksonian epilepsy, and hystero-epilepsy (psychic epilepsy). Differential diagnosis, causation, frequency of attacks, differentiation, treatment, occurrence, cure, heredity, epileptic behavior, and mental effects of epilepsy in child and adults are discussed. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved) 
General conclusions and discussion. $$$ The results of this study, as presented in the preceding chapters, do not confirm the hypothesis tested. That is, psychomotor epileptics were not demonstrated to display a greater incidence of functional psychiatric disorders than did control groups. For reasons to be mentioned later, it cannot be said that the hypothesis was completely disproved. Before dealing with the question of functional disorders, however, it seems appropriate first to consider the question of psychological disorders related to organic brain malfunction. Results in this area were the most unexpected and clinically significant encountered. A discussion of the bases for claiming validity for these findings is necessary. All of this leads to our final point about the finding of organic brain syndromes, which is to state explicitly that we do not know the etiology of the organicity we have reported. One obvious possibility is that it may be a drug effect. This would be consistent with the fact that the psychomotor subjects took more drugs and showed more organicity than the grand mal subjects. Another possibility may be the occurrence of subclinical seizures, as postulated by many clinicians. Finally, the locations of the epileptogenic foci should be mentioned as one possible source of variable impairment of mental functioning. This is rather difficult to credit, since in these cases gross structural lesions have been excluded. The identity among the Psychomotor Group, the Grand Mal Group, and the combined convulsive group in results from the scale dealing with maladaptation was very impressive. Each showed maladaptation in the area of sex, and in relationships with parents, siblings, and boss, as compared to the Medical Illnesses Group. Statistically significant differences occurred only for these four items. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved) 
Psychological observations. $$$ This chapter describes the administration of batteries of tests to the patients with epilepsy (the experimental subjects [psychomotor epilepsy or Grand Mal epilepsy]), as well as the comparison group of subjects with general medical illnesses. The findings were as follows: 1. All three groups display severe personality disturbance, primarily of a non-psychotic nature. 2. The three groups do not differ from the normal (average) nor from each other in overall intellectual functioning and memory. 3. In overall personality disturbance the two epileptic groups do not differ significantly, but both are slightly more disturbed than is the Medical Illnesses Group. 4. In regard to organic factors influencing psychological functioning, both epileptic groups displayed more evidence of this than did the Medical Illnesses Group, but the influence of these factors, even in the epileptic groups, was minimal. The Psychomotor Group is probably more affected by organic factors than is the Grand Mal Group, but the differences are slight. 5. There are marked differences in the incidence of different kinds of personality disturbances in the three groups. The Medical Illnesses Group is heavily saturated with neurotics and the Grand Mal Group with personality disorders. The Psychomotor Group displayed less personality disorder than the Grand Mal Group and contained fewer neurotics than the Medical Illnesses Group. The incidence of psychosis was greater in the Psychomotor than in the other two groups, with a small difference between the Psychomotor and Grand Mal Groups and a somewhat larger difference between the Psychomotor and Medical Illnesses Groups. 6. On a test of immediate recall both epileptic groups display a peculiarity of functioning, with the Psychomotor Group more affected. This does not appear to be associated with overall memory deficit. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved) 
Psychiatric observations. $$$ Each subject (with epilepsy) was examined independently by two psychiatrists. The interviews can be described as semi-structured in the sense that rating scales had to be completed at the end of each session. For the most part, however, the one and one-half to two hour interviews were conducted freely and according to the style of each examiner. The rating scales required the psychiatrist to make a large number of predetermined observations and judgments about the patient. In addition, each psychiatrist wrote a description of the patient's personality, emphasizing his characteristic adaptive and defensive patterns. The ratings on predetermined items were adapted to statistical comparison of the characteristics of the three diagnostic groups. The spontaneous description of the patient was used in arriving at a clinical diagnosis for each patient. Findings indicate that all three groups were significantly disturbed psychiatrically. The psychomotor patients showed symptoms which related to organic brain malfunction and fearfulness. The Grand Mal Group showed symptoms related to organic brain malfunction and an aggressive, suspicious, blaming others attitude. The Medical Illnesses Group showed some evidence of fearfulness and a pronounced tendency to experience bodily symptoms. The diagnostic data confirm the conclusions from the rating scales in an impressive way, and lead to the following general statements: 1. All of the diagnostic groups were composed of subjects with a very high incidence of psychiatric disturbance; roughly 90 percent of each of the groups merited a diagnosis of neurosis, psychosis, or personality disorder. 2. The high incidence of organic brain syndrome in the Psychomotor Group, indicated from the analysis of predetermined items, was confirmed in this evaluation, as was the lesser but distinct incidence in the Grand Mal Group. 3. The very high incidence of a diagnosis of personality disorder in the Grand Mal Group is consistent with the itemized findings of aggressiveness, suspiciousness, negativism, etc., and represents a tendency toward externalization of psychological tension. 4. In terms of functional emotional disturbances, the Psychomotor Group was diagnostically intermediate between the other two. It showed a greater incidence of personality disorder and less of neurosis than did the Medical Illnesses Group, but a greater incidence of neurosis and less of personality disturbance than did the Grand Mal Group. 5. The Psychomotor and Medical Illnesses Groups had statistically comparable rates of psychosis, whereas the grand mal subjects rarely merited this diagnosis. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved) 
Materials and methods of study. $$$ The principal goal of this study was to test the hypothesis that people with psychomotor epilepsy are more often disturbed psychiatrically than are those with other chronic illnesses. The method was to give neurological, psychiatric, and psychological examinations to three groups of subjects, and then to make comparisons from the data. The groups were: 1) thirty-two patients with psychomotor epilepsy; 2) twenty-six patients with idiopathic grand mal epilepsy; 3) twenty-six patients with a variety of chronic medical illnesses not involving the brain. The idiopathic grand mal epilepsy group was chosen to control for the possible effects of a convulsive disorder on the brain and the personality, and for reactions to social attitudes toward convulsive disorders. The group with chronic medical illnesses was chosen to control for the effects of the existence of chronic illness per se in the absence of any brain disorder. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved)
